summary:
Mars Field Guide is a free web app that plans astronaut surface walks (EVAs) on real Mars terrain. The user picks points on a map of Jezero Crater (Perseverance) or Mount Sharp (Curiosity) and sets limits for maximum slope, EVA length and time at each stop. The app then calculates the safest walking route and shows distance, time budget, reserve, radiation dose, an elevation profile, rock units and minerals at each stop, and photos the rover took nearby.

For the Martian Map challenge, it brings together data that is usually scattered across many archives:
- USGS terrain models
- NASA Mars Trek imagery
- CRISM mineral maps
- USGS geologic maps
- NASA DONKI and NOAA space weather
- Perseverance and Curiosity weather and raw images

Moving the slope slider shades on the map the ground too steep to walk, and the route updates automatically.

This matters because every hour outside costs a crew time and radiation dose: Curiosity measured about 0.64 mSv per day on the surface. With NASA moving from the Moon to Mars, planners need tools to test EVAs on real terrain before anyone lands.
details:
What it does and how it works

Mars Field Guide is a web app that plans astronaut walks (EVAs) on real Mars terrain at two sites: Jezero Crater (Perseverance) and Mount Sharp in Gale Crater (Curiosity). The user clicks waypoints on a satellite map and sets the maximum slope, EVA duration and time at each stop.

The backend turns USGS elevation models (16–20 m cells) into a walking-cost grid from slope, roughness and a thermal proxy, and blocks ground steeper than the limit. A least-cost path search finds the route. Walking time uses Tobler's hiking function, slowed by half for a pressure suit, which is our stated assumption. The radiation estimate uses Curiosity's measured surface dose of 0.64 mSv/day.

The results show:

- distance, total time and reserve

- radiation estimate and an elevation profile

- warnings

- the rock unit and CRISM mineral readings at each stop

- raw rover photos taken near each stop

Moving the slope slider shades too-steep ground in red on the map, and an existing route re-plans automatically. A space-weather panel turns NASA DONKI and NOAA GOES data into a go / caution / no-go status. A weather panel shows the latest rover weather report and says how old it is. Plans can be saved and shared by link.

Benefits

- Data from 7 separate NASA/USGS/NOAA sources comes together in one plan.

- Mission planners can test routes and timing before anyone lands.

- Scientists can choose stops by geology and minerals.

- Students can explore real Mars data for free in any browser, on desktop or phone.

Intended impact

Every hour outside costs a crew time and radiation dose. As NASA moves from the Moon to Mars, EVA planning tools need to be tested on real terrain early. The project uses only open data, and a new site needs one config file plus a public terrain model, so it can grow to more Mars sites and to Artemis landing sites on the Moon.

Tools and technologies

- Backend: Python, FastAPI, NumPy, scikit-image, SQLAlchemy/Alembic, PostgreSQL, Redis cache.

- Data pipeline: rasterio, pyproj, shapely and Pillow, to build the site data.

- Frontend: TypeScript, React, Vite, Leaflet.

- Infrastructure: Docker, Render (hosting), GitHub Actions (CI).

- Tests: 182 backend and 27 frontend automated tests.

- AI: Claude Code (Anthropic), used for coding, review and testing. The team reviewed every change.

- Hardware: no special hardware: personal laptops and free cloud hosting.

Creativity

Existing tools show Mars data one layer at a time. Ours joins terrain, minerals, geology, rover photos and space weather into one plan you can act on. Constraints are visible: drag the slope limit and you see the passable ground change. Plans are tied to the actual rover sites, so a planned stop can be compared with what the rover really saw there.

Factors we considered

- Scientific honesty: every assumption (suit speed, cost weights) is labelled, sources are linked, and old data is marked as old.

- Reliability: if a NASA feed fails, the app falls back to NOAA data or the last good result instead of breaking. Responses are cached.

- Safety and security: no secrets in code, rate limits, and no unauthenticated delete actions.

- Usability: clear error messages (for example "route not possible" with a hint) and a layout that works on phones.

- Cost: everything runs on free hosting.
